items.original_title: Intra-Asia rates soften as congestion at major ports begins to ease
items.summary: Intra-Asia rates are receding from their recent highs as bottlenecks in major Chinese and other Asian ports subside. On 15 October, Drewry’s Intra-Asia Container Index dipped 3%, to an average of $1,453 per 40ft. Rates from Shanghai to key destinations, including Busan in South Korea, Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam, and Jawaharlal Nehru Port in India, softened as vessel waiting times declined. Rates from Shanghai to Nhava Sheva fell 11%, to $3,370 per 40ft, while those to Busan declined 8% to $1,000 per 40ft. Shanghai–Singapore rates dropped 7% to $1,973 per 40ft. Port congestion eased during Week 41, with average vessel waiting times at Busan at 23 hours, from 26 hours a week earlier. At Jawaharlal Nehru Port, waiting times declined to 24 hours, from 42, and Singapore recorded a decrease to 34 hours, from 50. However, the deteriorating situation in the Middle East continued to support freight rates on the Shanghai–Jebel Ali route, which remained elevated, at $8,416 per 40ft. Freight rates from Busan to Shanghai rose 4%, to $159 per 40ft, with Yokohama to Shanghai up 4%, to $120 per 40ft.

items.title: Goldman Sachs sees crude freight rates surge to $20 per barrel
items.original_title: Goldman Sachs sees crude freight rates surge to $20 per barrel
items.summary: Global average crude freight rates have climbed above $20 per barrel from $3 per barrel a year ago, according to Goldman Sachs analysis released Wednesday. The increase initially started in the very large crude carrier segment and on Middle Eastern routes before spreading to all major crude trading routes, particularly affecting long-haul voyages. The bank identified five main drivers behind the $20 per barrel year-over-year surge in the average global crude freight rate. A war risk premium in Hormuz accounts for $7 per barrel, representing one-third of the increase in the global average crude freight rate. Inefficient tanker allocation and increased tanker redirections account for $3 per barrel, and the blockage of the Iranian fleet adds $2 per barrel by boosting demand for non-sanctioned crude tankers. Goldman Sachs expects these factors to continue supporting global freight rates as long as the conflict in the Middle East persists. The bank noted that high freight rates may reduce refiners’ overall demand for crude or shift it towards more closely located crude suppliers. Goldman Sachs sees high freight rates widening crude price differentials by changing crude trading patterns and supporting refined product prices while suppressing refiners’ net margins.

However, of the 21 initiatives identified by the end of June this year, 12 were still at the initiation stage, five were exploring feasibility, three had reached preparation and just one had entered the realisation phase. Chinese projects under development are targeting annual production of 30m tonnes of green methanol and 15m tonnes of green ammonia by the early 2030s, although the report cautions that not all announced capacity will reach the investment stage. The report found that green methanol and ammonia still cost two to three times as much as conventional marine fuels, even with China’s competitive production costs. items.summary: India’s crude oil import bill surged 46.3 percent to $90.6 billion during April–September on higher global prices even as volumes remained largely flat from the year-ago period, data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) shows. On October 21, Brent crude was trading higher at around $110 a barrel on supply concerns, with traders wary of Red Sea shipping risks and threats to oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia from Iran-backed Houthi rebels. India imported 122.7 million tonnes of oil during April-September, largely unchanged from 121.8 million tonnes in the previous year. In September, the import bill jumped 46.6 percent to $15.4 billion, while volumes were up 6.8 percent at 21.7 million tonnes. The average price of Indian crude basket has risen to $121.25 a barrel in October from $65.08 from last year. The bigger risk for India is not the availability of crude but persistently higher landed prices that can inflate the import bill, widen the current account deficit and weigh on the broader economy, analysts say. The country imports around 1.8-2 billion barrels of crude annually and every $1-a-barrel increase in price raises the country’s import bill by up to $2 billion a year.

items.summary: Energy and commodities trading group BGN has ordered four 93,000-cbm LPG-capable gas carriers from HD Hyundai Heavy Industries for delivery in January 2030. BGN signed the contract for the four very large gas carriers (VLGCs) with South Korean shipbuilder HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (HD HHI) in Istanbul. The ships will be able to run on LPG or conventional marine fuel. The new ships will take BGN’s owned VLGC fleet from 19 to 23 once delivered. Including the latest order, BGN has ordered 10 dual-fuel VLGCs from HD HHI in 2026 so far. In April, it ordered four 90,000-cbm dual-fuel VLGCs that can run on conventional and lower-emission fuels and carry ammonia, with delivery by 2029. In September, BGN agreed a long-term time charter with Japanese tanker operator IINO Kaiun Kaisha (IINO Lines) for a 90,000-cbm LPG dual-fuel VLGC. Other gas carrier owners have also ordered LPG-capable ships. There are currently 183 LPG dual-fuel vessels in operation globally, with another 165 such vessels on order through 2030, according to DNV data.

items.title: Panama Canal Traffic and Tonnage Rise Despite El Niño Challenges
items.original_title: Panama Canal Traffic and Tonnage Rise Despite El Niño Challenges
items.summary: The Panama Canal reported growth in vessel traffic, tonnage and revenue in fiscal year 2026, as stronger demand from energy carriers and containerships helped lift volumes despite ongoing concerns over water availability. The waterway handled 13,951 vessel transits during the fiscal year ended September 30, up 4.1% from 13,404 the previous year, according to results released Wednesday by the Panama Canal Authority. Total tonnage climbed 6.5% to 521 million Panama Canal Universal Measurement System (PC/UMS) tons, compared with 489.2 million tons in fiscal 2025. The results come as the canal continues to balance growing shipping demand with water conservation measures designed to protect operations during the developing El Niño weather pattern. Despite the challenges, the canal maintained a maximum authorized draft of 50 feet throughout the fiscal year’s dry season, providing relatively stable operating conditions for shipping customers. “Far from restricting trade flows, the Panama Canal facilitates international maritime trade by providing its customers with a reliable and safe route,” Panama Canal Administrator Ilya Espino de Marotta said during a conference call hosted by Bank of America Merrill Lynch. The canal has warned that a continuing water deficit could require further operational adjustments, particularly if El Niño conditions intensify.

Army Photo By Chris Servello (OpEd) After years of testing and debating how unmanned surface vessels fit into the fleet, the Navy is starting to show what these systems can do. And senior leaders in the Department of War and Department of the Navy are talking less about the promise of unmanned warfare and more about making it part of everyday operations. The Navy needs to decide how it intends to fight with unmanned vessels, what missions they’ll perform and how it will organize, train and sustain the forces operating them. It’s time to move from proving these systems work to making them a routine part of fleet operations. For years, Task Force 59 worked with industry and regional partners to introduce unmanned systems into one of the world’s toughest maritime environments. The deployment of the Leidos-built Seahawk medium unmanned surface vessel with the Theodore Roosevelt strike group is another important step.

items.title: Follow the money or follow the flag? Politics clouds port investment
items.original_title: Follow the money or follow the flag? Politics clouds port investment
items.summary: In the seven years since TOC Americas last took place in Cartagena, global laden container volumes have slipped about 10% below where they would have been without the multiple disruptions that have hit the industry since 2018, according to Dinesh Sharma, director at Drewry Maritime Advisors. Sharma’s research measured growth from 2018 against forecasts of where the industry had imagined it would be today last time they met in Cartagena. Predicting the future, he said, was and is not easy. Transshipment hubs grew by about 6% a year on average over that period, against roughly 3% for gateway ports and 1.5% for the underlying economies they serve. The inefficiency, he said, is no longer contained at the big transshipment hubs: it is flowing through to gateways too, leaving Latin America’s overall throughput an estimated 2–3% below his 2018 projection. Washington’s growing interest in the region’s infrastructure raises the odds that port decisions get caught up in politics rather than commercial logic.

items.title: European gas rallies on Persian gulf disruption pressure; Hot UK Inflation dents
items.original_title: European gas rallies on Persian gulf disruption pressure; Hot UK Inflation dents
items.summary: European wholesale natural gas prices surged on Wednesday, with both major regional benchmarks gaining over 3% as hotter-than-expected British inflation data and ongoing Persian Gulf energy disruptions heightened anxieties over winter fuel adequacy. The benchmark Dutch TTF front-month contract rose 3.1% to trade at 87.95 euros per megawatt-hour (MWh). In Great Britain, the equivalent NBP natural gas futures contract similarly advanced 3.2% to 216.57 pence per therm, with both contracts holding near their highest levels since late 2022. Wednesday’s gas rally coincided with fresh macroeconomic data highlighting the acute economic toll of elevated energy import costs on the British economy. Official figures showed Britain’s annual consumer price inflation accelerated to 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August and exceeding market consensus. Lacking large-scale long-term gas storage infrastructure, the UK relies heavily on real-time imports of pipeline gas and Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) cargoes to meet domestic power generation and home heating needs. The European benchmark remains up approximately 210% year-to-date. With maritime strikes and transit friction restricting LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz – keeping Middle Eastern deliveries to Europe nearly 80% below year-ago levels—European utilities face intense competition from Asian buyers for uncommitted Atlantic basin cargoes.

items.original_title: IEA: Gulf Oil Shipping Costs Top $37 Per Barrel, Five Times Pre-War Levels
items.summary: FILE PHOTO: Crude oil tanker Odessa, carrying UAE crude after passing through the Strait of Hormuz with its Automatic Identification System transponder turned off, navigates the waters at Daesan port, where it is expected to discharge crude oil, in Seosan, South Korea, May 8, 2026. REUTERS/Kim Soo-hyeon/File Photo The cost of shipping crude oil from the Middle East Gulf to Asia has surged to more than $37 per barrel, over five times prewar levels, as an increasingly complex shipping network keeps oil flowing despite escalating Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the International Energy Agency. The extraordinary increase comes as Persian Gulf oil exports have actually surpassed prewar levels, highlighting the steep price of maintaining energy flows through one of the world’s most dangerous shipping corridors. According to The Wall Street Journal , citing vessel-tracking data from Kpler, Middle East oil shipments averaged more than 24 million barrels per day in the week ending October 18, exceeding the prewar average of 23.3 million barrels per day. In a separate analysis published Wednesday , the IEA said tanker rates reached historic highs in September and continued climbing into October, with the cost of transporting crude from the Middle East Gulf to Asia exceeding $37 per barrel by mid-month.

items.title: Nearly two-thirds of Far East-Europe capacity now back to Suez Canal
items.original_title: Nearly two-thirds of Far East-Europe capacity now back to Suez Canal
items.summary: Some 63% of the ocean capacity deployed between the Far East and Europe has returned to the Red Sea, following three years of detours, but some operators are hedging against renewed disruption by maintaining several Cape of Good Hope routes. Having surveyed the 10 largest carrier networks over the past month, Alphaliner found vessels on 24 of the 46 direct Far East–Europe services were transiting the Red Sea, accounting for 70% of deployed capacity on Far East-Mediterranean routes. On the Far East-North Europe trades, the number was a little lower, 58%, with containers moving between the Far East and Europe via Suez now topping 5.5m teu, of the possible 8.7m teu available to the trades – CMA CGM alone accounting for 1.3m of this. However, the Suez return remains something of a mixed bag, with multiple services opting to transit the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait on outbound routes to Europe, but electing to sail around the Cape on return journeys. Of the 10 carriers surveyed, five confirmed they had resumed Red Sea transits over the past month, that number set to climb to eight after Premier Alliance partners HMM, ONE, and Yang Ming all announced a return to the waterway.

items.original_title: Airfreight in Africa booming, thanks to disrupted ocean shipping services
items.summary: African airfreight is seeing something of a boom from the disruption in ocean freight across the Middle East, but forwarders remain sceptical as to whether it will provoke long-term structural benefits. Hennie Heymans, CEO of DHL Express’s Sub-Saharan Africa operations, told The Loadstar the shift from ocean services had left airfreight the only viable alternative to keep goods moving. “When people run into trouble from a seafreight point of view, the alternative becomes airfreight, becomes express, and that is a notable trend across African airfreight’s growth momentum at the moment,” Mr Heymans told The Loadstar . For DHL Express, the timing has proved particularly useful, coinciding with the launch of its Heavy Weight Express service, allowing its customers to ship consignments of up to 3,000kg, with individual pieces of up to 1,000kg. Expanding beyond smaller parcels, the new service is designed for automotive, energy, engineering, machinery, and pharmaceuticals, Mr Heymans noting the significant cost implications delays place on these sectors. “The timing of the launch worked out quite well, which makes the conversation a lot easier, and a lot more comfortable for those customers seeking these sorts of services,” explained Mr Heymans.

items.original_title: Ports Are Scaling AI. Here’s How to Make It Deliver
items.summary: Ports and terminals are no strangers to reinvention. Over the past 50 years, the industry has managed and adapted to the shift to containerization and ever-larger vessels, the move from paper manifests to electronic messaging and transactions, and the subsequent evolution to system-to-system integration with other parties in the shipping industries. But many port functions still run on clipboards, radio calls, or the gut instincts of a planner, who has watched the yard fill up and empty thousands of times. To assess how far the industry has come, BCG and TIC4.0 (an international nonprofit association of terminal operators and equipment and solution providers dedicated to the creation and promotion of digital standards for the cargo-handling industry) surveyed more than 100 leaders from across the container ports and terminals ecosystem. On average, those we surveyed are already using or exploring the top 16 of the 43 use cases we assessed, from extracting data from shipping documents (62%) to predicting when a crane or straddle carrier will fail (48%). Survey Demographics In August 2026, BCG and the Terminal Industry Committee 4.0 (TIC4.0) surveyed the port and terminal ecosystem on the adoption of AI and generative AI, to establish where the industry sees the opportunity and where it sees the risk.

ESI 2.0 updates this framework to reflect developments in regulation, technology and vessel operations, with increased recognition of areas including energy use, greenhouse gas performance, innovation and electrification. ESI 2.0 reflects the priorities of shipping today As shipping adopts cleaner fuels, electrification and new emissions-reduction technologies, the way environmental performance is measured also needs to evolve. Port of Aarhus turns the new methodology into action To understand the impact of ESI 2.0, OceanScore analysed Port of Aarhus’ 2025 vessel calls and how its existing incentive scheme would perform under the updated methodology. Keeping incentives effective as shipping evolves The Aarhus example demonstrates how ports can respond to changes in environmental performance measurement while keeping their incentive schemes relevant to the vessels they serve. “ESI 2.0 reflects how environmental priorities in shipping are evolving, and the Aarhus example shows how ports can translate that into practical incentives,” says Thomas Smith, Head of Cargo Solutions at OceanScore.

items.title: Disconnected systems and AI hype are driving digital fatigue in shipping, warns OrbitMI
items.original_title: Disconnected systems and AI hype are driving digital fatigue in shipping, warns OrbitMI
items.summary: Shipping’s drive to digitalise risks slowing itself down as fragmented software, weak digital training and growing pressure to adopt artificial intelligence add complexity to operational and commercial decisions, according to OrbitMI. OrbitMI warns that the sector is entering a period of ‘digital fatigue’: growing scepticism and frustration when technology fails to deliver the promised simplicity or measurable productivity and performance improvement gains. After years of adding platforms and bolt-on applications, many teams still transfer data manually, work across separate dashboards and adapt established processes to generic interfaces. Research by Thetius and Marcura found that 82% of maritime professionals believe AI can improve efficiency and 81% are running pilots, but only 11% have the policies and governance needed to scale it. Two-thirds are concerned that overreliance on AI could erode human judgement, while 69% worry it may miss critical red flags in contracts or voyage planning. What users need are tools that are truly collaborative and are fully integrated in their workflows; always present but never intrusive. OrbitMI has been investing in this approach through the acquisition of AI specialist AuQub and maritime advisory and voyage optimisation business Gale Force, alongside the expansion of its maritime, product and technology leadership over the past 18 months.

items.title: HarborLab: Why shipping’s husbandry bills are still stuck in Excel
items.original_title: HarborLab: Why shipping’s husbandry bills are still stuck in Excel
items.summary: Shipping has spent years tightening voyage costs, bunker procurement and commercial port expenses, but one sizeable part of the bill remains comparatively untouched: husbandry. For Antonis Malaxianakis, founder and CEO of Athens-based port cost management platform HarborLab, that blind spot is particularly evident around bunkering, crew changes and stores, where technical departments can still be managing substantial sums through spreadsheets and email. “Husbandry calls have never carried the same profit and loss visibility as commercial port calls,” Malaxianakis tells Maritime CEO. For Malaxianakis, who worked in disbursement departments at Thenamaris and Product Shipping & Trading before founding HarborLab in 2020, the problem is less about a lack of attention from technical managers than the tools available to them. “One data point from our analysis makes the structural difference concrete: 75% of technical managers in APAC still manage husbandry bills in Excel today, compared with 40% in EMEA,” he says. The HarborLab-managed vessels generated $220,000 in savings compared with $70,000 on the other half. The system also picks up incorrect and duplicated charges, with the company then taking discrepancies back to agents in an effort to turn the finding into a credit. Behind that sits a database built from more than 40,000 port calls across over 1,400 ports.

items.summary: Amid the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a 19th South Korean oil tanker is transporting crude oil to South Korea via a Red Sea detour. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries announced that as of 10 a.m. on Oct. 20, one South Korean vessel had loaded crude oil at Yanbu Port in Saudi Arabia and was heading to South Korea after passing through the Suez Canal. This shipment is the 19th case of crude transport via the Red Sea since the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz began at the end of February. South Korean oil tankers had originally, from April, loaded crude at Yanbu Port on the Red Sea and entered South Korea via the southern Bab el-Mandeb Strait. As the closure of the Strait of Hormuz becomes prolonged, detour shipments to secure domestic energy supply are expected to continue for the time being. So far, a total of 19 South Korean vessels have transported crude oil through the Red Sea. The government said it is continuously monitoring the safe operation of vessels and managing the situation to prevent disruptions in crude oil supply.

The measure — detailed on Monday, just weeks ahead of the US midterm elections — is the latest in a string of efforts by the Trump administration to cool crude and fuel prices driven higher by months of war in the Persian Gulf and the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine. But with limited numbers of sanctioned supertankers actually available and would-be sellers unwilling to forgo lucrative crossings in the Middle East, industry analysts say the effort to revive so-called dark vessels may struggle to gain traction. “The number of vessels that could realistically migrate back into mainstream trading would likely be materially smaller than the overall sanctioned fleet.” Under the US proposal, blacklisted vessels can be sold and rejoin the legitimate fleet, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Monday, adding the government would “convert” tankers to expand global availability but would not lift existing sanctions.

items.title: Kpler Expands ‘Dark Fleet’ Tracking With Airbus Satellite Deal
items.original_title: Kpler Expands ‘Dark Fleet’ Tracking With Airbus Satellite Deal
items.summary: A satellite image of side-by-side ships at sea, off the coast of Sohar, Oman, June 9, 2026. SPOT © CNES 2026, Distribution Airbus DS/Handout via REUTERS Maritime data provider Kpler has reached an agreement with Airbus to expand its ability to track vessels that disappear from conventional ship-tracking systems, adding daily satellite imagery to help identify ships operating without reliable Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals. The agreement, announced Tuesday , will integrate imagery from Airbus’s SPOT Earth observation satellites with Kpler’s existing vessel-tracking network, allowing analysts to detect ships independently of their reported AIS positions. The service will use high-resolution satellite imagery, with a resolution of 1.5 meters and a 60-kilometer swath, combined with artificial intelligence to identify vessels at sea and in port. The technology is intended to address a growing challenge for maritime tracking: determining whether a vessel has deliberately switched off or manipulated its AIS signal, or whether its reported position has been affected by interference with satellite navigation systems. By comparing AIS data with independently captured satellite imagery, Kpler says it can better distinguish between the two. Gordon said combining AIS information with satellite imagery and other independent sources would give shipping companies and governments a clearer picture of maritime activity, particularly when vessels disappear from electronic tracking systems.

items.summary: The European Union unveiled a new Arctic strategy Tuesday aimed at strengthening maritime security, expanding icebreaker capacity and protecting critical infrastructure as melting sea ice opens new shipping routes and geopolitical competition intensifies across the region. The strategy , the EU’s first major update since 2021, marks a shift toward security and economic interests in a region increasingly important to global shipping, trade and energy supplies. At the center of the plan is a proposed Maritime Security Hub designed to improve surveillance and information sharing across the Arctic, including the monitoring and protection of critical undersea infrastructure. Von der Leyen pointed to Russia’s growing military presence in the Arctic, increasing pressure on regional security and the emergence of new shipping routes as reasons for Europe to take a more active role. The EU also plans to expand its use of satellite monitoring and data sharing, including a dedicated Arctic surveillance pilot scheduled for 2027 to improve maritime domain awareness. New shipping routes could create opportunities for ports, logistics providers and shipbuilders, but Arctic operations remain constrained by ice conditions, limited infrastructure, environmental risks and the availability of emergency response capabilities.

Unlike major Chinese gateways such as Shanghai and Ningbo-Zhoushan, which benefit from substantial domestic volumes, Singapore relies heavily on transhipment traffic and its role as a connecting hub for global shipping lines. The new port is expected to have an annual handling capacity of 65m teu by the 2040s, with technology playing a central role in increasing throughput and maximising productivity, amid the country’s land constraints. items.title: UK shipowners warn against copying FuelEU red tape
items.original_title: UK shipowners warn against copying FuelEU red tape
items.summary: The UK Chamber of Shipping has urged the British government to avoid repeating the compliance problems encountered under FuelEU Maritime as it prepares to introduce its own maritime fuel standard. In a policy paper published this week, the industry body warned that the EU regime, which came into force in January 2025, had imposed a substantially greater administrative workload on shipowners and regulators than initially anticipated. The 22-page report identifies difficulties with reporting deadlines, fuel certification, emissions calculations and compliance pooling arrangements. The Chamber wants the UK government to establish a fully tested ship-level monitoring and reporting system before introducing compliance obligations. Peter Aylott, the Chamber’s director of policy, said the government had an opportunity to learn from the EU’s experience rather than create another regulatory system that increased costs and complexity. The paper also calls for close alignment with emerging International Maritime Organization requirements to avoid duplicate certification, reporting and verification obligations. The intervention comes as the Department for Transport prepares to consult on a domestic maritime fuel standard, with the consultation expected later this year. Britain’s maritime decarbonisation strategy, unveiled in March 2025, targets a 30% reduction in domestic shipping’s lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by 2030, rising to 80% by 2040 and zero by 2050, against a 2008 baseline.

items.title: Northern Sea Route smashes shipping records again
items.original_title: Northern Sea Route smashes shipping records again
items.summary: Shipping along Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) has already broken last year’s transit record. New figures from Norway’s Centre for High North Logistics (CHNL) show 104 confirmed transits by September 30, surpassing the 103 recorded during the whole of 2025 and 97 in 2024. Estimated transit cargo reached 3.7m tonnes, up 15% on the whole of last year, while the combined deadweight of vessels using the route increased 26% to 7.8m dwt. CHNL identified another 45 potential transits already underway or within the route at the end of September, suggesting the season could approach 150 voyages and more than 4.5m tonnes of cargo. Four direct Asia-Europe voyages had been completed by September 30, compared with just one during the whole of last year. Russian oil exports through the NSR have climbed nearly 50% this year, with approximately 20m barrels shipped to Asia between July and mid-October. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, Suez Canal and Black Sea has made the expensive and potentially hazardous Arctic passage increasingly attractive. Russian LNG shipments are also contributing to traffic growth, with CHNL recording four eastbound LNG cargoes totalling approximately 300,000 tonnes.

The organisation has recorded 354 enclosed space accidents over the past 30 years, between 1996 and 2026, across tankers, bulkers, general cargo ships, passenger vessels, containerships and other vessel types. Its latest seafarer survey identifies a recurring gap between safety procedures and operational reality onboard. InterManager says this must now be enhanced to deliver competence, rather than just training, particularly as enclosed space entry training is being considered as part of the current review of STW requirements, with the International Chamber of Shipping leading industry input. InterManager will explore the survey findings and wider enclosed space safety concerns during a webinar, run in conjunction with The Nautical Institute, on 27 October 2026 at 10am GMT. The webinar will bring together industry experts, Captain Pradeep Chawla, CEO of Marie Pals, Captain Garry Hallett from InterManager and Richard Cowburn, human factors specialist, to discuss where the industry stands now on enclosed space safety, how seafarers and shore-based stakeholders feel about current practice, and what practical action is needed next.

The report reflects AD Ports Group’s gains in mitigating the environmental impact of its integrated global trade, transport, logistics, and economic development activities, through measures such as increased operating efficiencies and the use of solar electricity, lower-impact maritime fuels, and electric-powered vessels. The Group’s total emissions intensity, which calculates tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e) per AED 1 million in revenue across emissions Scopes 1, 2 and 3, fell by 6% to 190.68 tCO₂e in 2025 from 203.06 tCO₂e in 2024. In 2025, the Group adopted a decarbonisation pathway covering its operations and value chain, with 139 initiatives planned between 2025 and 2050. The Group continued to advance its decarbonisation journey as the business grew robustly in 2025, reducing the total emissions intensity of our business per AED 1 million of revenue by 6% from 2024 levels through greater efficiencies and the use of solar and alternative energy.

items.title: Danica Urges Shipping Industry to Manage Crew Turnover, Not Just Retention
items.original_title: Danica Urges Shipping Industry to Manage Crew Turnover, Not Just Retention
items.summary: Shipping companies need to pay as much attention to managing crew turnover as they do to retaining seafarers if they are to maintain safe and efficient vessel operations, according to Henrik Jensen, founder and CEO of Danica Crewing Specialists. Speaking ahead of this week’s Crew Connect Global 2026 in Manila (20-22 October), Mr Jensen warned that while retaining experienced seafarers remains a priority, changing attitudes towards employment mean shipowners and managers must accept that some crew turnover is inevitable and be better prepared to manage it. “Having a stable crew pool makes a significant difference to the safe and efficient operation of a vessel. We also need to think about how we manage these changes when they happen.” Mr Jensen explained that traditional retention strategies, including competitive salaries, bonuses, insurance, pensions and promotion opportunities, have largely been built around the expectations of older generations, who tend to value stability and long-term employment. Mr Jensen believes shipping companies should focus on making it easier for new crew members to familiarise themselves with onboard equipment, procedures and working practices.

items.title: Who owns shipping’s carbon decisions?
items.original_title: Who owns shipping’s carbon decisions?
items.summary: In an industry where a position list is a competitive weapon, the question is no longer just how to comply—but where carbon decisions are made and who controls the data behind them, said Argyris Zafeiropoulos, principal advisor at Resilience & Compliance Advisory. With the EU Emissions Trading System fully phased into shipping and FuelEU Maritime tightening year by year, carbon is now a line item in every fixture. On a single laden Aframax voyage from the Gulf to Rotterdam, the FuelEU penalty alone climbs to about €246,000 ($276,000) by 2040 — same ship, same route, same fuel. Far less attention goes to a quieter question: where are these carbon decisions actually made, and who can see the data behind them? On that voyage, ETS and FuelEU together come to about €104,000 ($116,600) at an €81 ($91) allowance price — roughly one euro ($1.12) on every tonne of a 100,000-tonne cargo, rising to about €1.36 ($1.53) by 2030. In commodity trades, the choice between CIF and FOB helps decide who absorbs it. Carbon has moved beyond the charter party and into the commodity contract. Shipping has always rewarded those who control their critical assets — ships, cargo relationships, market intelligence and commercial judgement.

items.original_title: Oil tanker on fire after hitting mine in Hormuz: Iran’s Guards
items.summary: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said Monday an oil tanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine, the latest such incident since Tehran tightened its grip of the waterway. Iran seized control of the strait after war broke out against the United States and Israel late February, choking off the vital shipping route which normally carries about a fifth of the world’s oil. The Islamic republic has demanded that all ships seek its authorisation before transiting. “An oil tanker, which was in violation, struck a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in an explosion and a fire in its engine room,” Iranian state media quoted the Guards as saying. The tanker was travelling in the strait’s “unauthorized southern route” and had disabled its positioning and navigation systems, the statement said. It came a day after the Guards said two oil tankers caught fire in the strait, both after hitting mines. The Guards’ naval commander Admiral Ali Ozmaei warned this week that any vessel that deactivated its navigation systems would be considered “hostile.” The United States has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian oil exports in response to Tehran’s blockade on the waterway. items.original_title: Solar power a shining example of export progress across sub-Saharan Africa
items.summary: Solar energy is becoming increasingly important for bolstering sub-Saharan Africa’s trading potential, with supply chain executives telling The Loadstar that Kenya and Nigeria are two of the fastest-growing markets for the technology. By the end of the first quarter, Nigeria had climbed into the top 10 of solar panel suppliers to the US, with some 40% of the country’s total exports of the technology, totalling $64bn, ending up in the US. That growth has been felt by forwarders and logistics partners. DHL Express’s chief executive for Sub-Saharan Africa, Hennie Heymans, told The Loadstar the company was seeing “incredible growth” in solar-panel exports out of Nigeria – and nor is that country alone. “We actually see an incredible growth in solar panel exports towards the United States from Nigeria and Kenya,” he said, pointing out that for Africa in general the “new energy” vertical was proving something of a winner, experiencing 20% growth year on year. items.original_title: Analysis: The ETS question – did carriers redesign Asia-Europe services to avoid carbon tax?
items.summary: Would a carrier really design its Asia-Europe network around shaving marginal ETS dollars, which it can recoup through surcharges anyway? In short, carriers did redesign for the ETS – though not around the ETS alone. Carriers have redesigned Asia–Europe loops to cut their exposure, and they were right to. A few months ago, the EU ETS Observatory published a report stating that UK volume growth was a direct result of shippers seeking to minimise the EU-ETS charges – bullocks, if you ask me. The first is above – carriers optimised their networks within the rules, as they were entitled to, and importers were spared hundreds of millions of euros a year: the Observatory puts the allowances not collected at the three UK ports alone at about €316m. It removes the carbon price from the Asia leg, the longest of the voyage, and with it any ETS reason to slow down or burn a bio-blend there. The commission’s carbon market report found about 5% of national ETS revenue went to industrial decarbonisation, and only France and Estonia ringfence a share for shipping. Its July proposal would create a reserve of up to 110m allowances from 2028 to 2040, covering 55%–90% of the price gap for sustainable fuels and zero-emission propulsion.
